title: Use a Graphical User Interface (GUI)-based spreadsheet application to create and edit spreadsheets

lessons.title: Getting to know the spreadsheet
lessons.html:
What a spreadsheet is

A spreadsheet is a computer program that arranges information in rows and columns. Examples are Microsoft Excel, LibreOffice Calc and Google Sheets. In a farm workshop you can use a spreadsheet to keep a list of tractors and their service hours, track parts in stock, record fuel use or work out the cost of a repair job.

Parts of the screen

  • Columns go up and down and have letters: A, B, C.
  • Rows go across and have numbers: 1, 2, 3.
  • A cell is one box where a column and row meet. Cell B3 is in column B, row 3.
  • The active cell has a thick border. This is where you type.
  • The formula bar shows what is in the active cell.
  • The ribbon or menu at the top has buttons for saving, formatting and more.
  • Sheet tabs at the bottom let you have more than one sheet in a file (a workbook).

Starting and saving

  1. Open the spreadsheet program and choose a blank workbook.
  2. Click on a cell and type. Press Enter to move down or Tab to move right.
  3. Save your file: click File, then Save As. Choose the correct folder and give it a clear name, such as Tractor service log 2026.
  4. Save often while you work using Ctrl+S.
  5. To open the file later, click File, then Open, and find it.

Using the mouse and keyboard

Click a cell to select it. Drag across cells to select a range, for example A1 to D1. Use the arrow keys to move one cell at a time. Double-click a cell to change what is in it, or select it and type to replace it. Press Esc to cancel.

lessons.title: Entering data and simple formulas
lessons.html:
Building a simple workshop sheet

Let us make a list of parts used on a tractor service.

ABCD
1PartQuantityPrice each (R)Total (R)
2Oil filter1320
3Engine oil (litre)1295
4Fuel filter2180

Types of data

  • Text (labels) such as 'Oil filter'.
  • Numbers such as 12 or 320.
  • Dates such as 2026/03/15.
  • Formulas that calculate an answer.

Writing formulas

Every formula starts with an equals sign (=). Use cell addresses instead of typing the numbers, so the answer updates if a number changes.

  • In D2 type =B2*C2 and press Enter. The answer is 320.
  • The symbols are: + add, − subtract, * multiply, / divide.
  • To copy the formula down, click D2, then drag the small square in the corner of the cell (the fill handle) down to D4. The formulas change to =B3*C3 and =B4*C4 by themselves.

Using SUM

In D5 type =SUM(D2:D4). This adds all cells from D2 to D4. The answer is 320 + 1 140 + 360 = R1 820. You can also use the AutoSum button.

Other useful functions: =AVERAGE(B2:B4), =MAX(C2:C4), =MIN(C2:C4).

Editing

To change data, click the cell and type the new value. Use Ctrl+Z to undo a mistake. To insert a row, right-click the row number and choose Insert. To delete, right-click and choose Delete.

lessons.title: Formatting, checking and printing
lessons.html:
Making the sheet easy to read

Formatting cells

  • Make headings bold and maybe fill them with a light colour.
  • Widen a column by double-clicking the line between column letters, so all text fits.
  • Format money cells as Currency so they show R and two decimals, such as R1 820.00.
  • Format date cells as Date.
  • Use Wrap Text when a heading is long.
  • Add borders around your table so it prints clearly.
  • Align numbers to the right and text to the left.

Sorting

To sort parts by name, select the table and click Sort A to Z. To sort by price, sort on that column. Always select the whole table, or the rows will mix up.

Checking your work

  • Check numbers you typed against the job card or invoice.
  • Click on formula cells and look at the formula bar to see that they point to the right cells.
  • Look out for error messages like #DIV/0! (dividing by zero) or #VALUE! (text where a number should be).
  • Make a rough estimate. If the total for three parts shows R182 000, something is wrong.

Printing

  1. Click File, then Print, and look at the preview.
  2. Choose portrait or landscape. Wide sheets often fit better in landscape.
  3. Use Fit to page width if columns are cut off.
  4. Add a header or footer with the sheet name and date if needed.
  5. Choose the printer and number of copies, then print.

Looking after files

Save in the correct folder, keep a backup and do not delete other people's sheets. Close the file when you are done.

Key points

  • A cell is named by its column letter and row number, such as B3.
  • Every formula starts with =; use cell addresses, not typed numbers.
  • =SUM(D2:D4) adds a range of cells.
  • Format money as Currency and make headings bold.
  • Check formulas and use print preview before printing.
  • Save often and use clear file names.
